questions.worked_solution:
According to the definition of the biconditional, 

- $P⇔Q$ is true if $P⇒Q$ **and** $Q⇒P.$ Otherwise, it is false.

- In other words, $P⇔Q$ is true if $P$ and $Q$ have the same truth values. Otherwise, it is false.

So, when $A=\text{F}$ and $B=\text{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(A⇔¬B) & =(\text{F}⇔¬\text{T}) \\  & =(\text{F}⇔\text{F}) \\  & =\text{T}.\end{aligned}
$$

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,¬B\,$ | $\,A⇔¬B\,$ |

questions.worked_solution:
According to the definition of the biconditional, 

- $P⇔Q$ is true if $P⇒Q$ **and** $Q⇒P.$ Otherwise, it is false.

- In other words, $P⇔Q$ is true if $P$ and $Q$ have the same truth values. Otherwise, it is false.

First, we add a column for $Y∨X:$

| $\,X\,$ | $\,Y\,$ | $\,Y∨X\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |

Then, we add a column for $(Y∨X)⇔X.$ 

| $\,X\,$ | $\,Y\,$ | $\,Y∨X\,$ | $\,(Y∨X)⇔X\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

questions.problem:
Find the missing values in the following truth table:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,(A∧B)⇔B\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | {{field-1}} |

| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | {{field-4}} |
questions.worked_solution:
According to the definition of the biconditional, 

- $P⇔Q$ is true if $P⇒Q$ **and** $Q⇒P.$ Otherwise, it is false.

- In other words, $P⇔Q$ is true if $P$ and $Q$ have the same truth values. Otherwise, it is false.

First, we add a column for $A∧B:$

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,A∧B\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |

Then, we add a column for $(A∧B)⇔B.$ 

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,A∧B\,$ | $\,(A∧B)⇔B\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |

Find the missing values in the following truth table:

| $\,X\,$ | $\,Y\,$ | $\,(X∧Y)⇔¬(X∨Y)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | {{field-1}} |

questions.worked_solution:
According to the definition of the biconditional, 

- $P⇔Q$ is true if $P⇒Q$ **and** $Q⇒P.$ Otherwise, it is false.

- In other words, $P⇔Q$ is true if $P$ and $Q$ have the same truth values. Otherwise, it is false.

First, we add columns for $X∧Y,$ $X∨Y,$ and $¬(X∨Y):$

| $\,X\,$ | $\,Y\,$ | $\,X∧Y\,$ | $\,X∨Y\,$ | $\,¬(X∨Y)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |

Example: 
                    Simplifying Expressions Involving Equivalences
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following statements are equivalent to $\lnot (\neg Y \Leftrightarrow Z)?$

I. $Y \Rightarrow \lnot Z$

II. $(Y \lor Z) \Rightarrow (Y \land Z)$

III. $(Y \land Z) \land (Y \land \lnot Z)$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we use the definition of the biconditional statement to write the equivalence as a conjunction of implications: 

$$
\lnot (\lnot Y \Leftrightarrow Z) 
\equiv \lnot \big[(\lnot Y \Rightarrow Z) \land (Z \Rightarrow \lnot Y)\big]
$$

Now, we represent all the implications using disjunctions and negations:

$$
\lnot \big[(\lnot Y \Rightarrow Z) \land (Z \Rightarrow \lnot Y)\big]
\equiv \lnot \big[(\lnot \lnot Y \lor Z) \land (\lnot Z \lor \lnot Y)\big]
$$

Next, we simplify the double negations:

$$
\lnot \big[(\lnot \lnot Y \lor Z) \land (\lnot Z \lor \lnot Y)\big] 
\equiv \lnot \big[(Y \lor Z) \land (\lnot Z \lor \lnot Y)\big]
$$

Now, we use De Morgan's laws:

$$
\begin{aligned}¬[(Y∨Z)∧(¬Z∨¬Y)] & ≡¬(Y∨Z)∨¬(¬Z∨¬Y) \\  & ≡¬(Y∨Z)∨¬¬(Z∧Y)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we again simplify the double negations and write down symbols in alphabetic order inside the parentheses using commutative laws:

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(Y∨Z)∨¬¬(Z∧Y) & ≡¬(Y∨Z)∨(Z∧Y) \\  & ≡¬(Y∨Z)∨(Y∧Z) \\  & ≡(Y∨Z)⇒(Y∧Z)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is only II.

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Of particular importance in mathematical proofs are so-called **biconditional statements.** These are statements of the form

$$
(P\Rightarrow Q) \land (Q\Rightarrow P).
$$

In words, a biconditional statement states that *"$P$ implies $Q,$ **and** $Q$ implies $P.$"* 

Let's construct a truth table for this biconditional statement.

| $\,P\,$ | $\,Q\,$ | $\,P\Rightarrow Q\,$ | $\,Q\Rightarrow P\,$ | $\,(P \Rightarrow Q)\land (Q \Rightarrow P)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |

Biconditional statements are so important that we give them a special symbol.

$$
P\Leftrightarrow Q
$$

So, we now have the following logical equivalence:

$$
P \Leftrightarrow Q \equiv (P \Rightarrow Q) \land (Q \Rightarrow P)
$$

The truth table for $P\Leftrightarrow Q$ is as follows:

| $\,P\,$ | $\,Q\,$ | $\,P\Leftrightarrow Q\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |

According to the truth table, $P\Leftrightarrow Q$ is true if $P$ and $Q$ have the *same* truth value. Otherwise, it is false. We can express this as another logical equivalence:

$$
P\Leftrightarrow Q \equiv \big(P \land Q\big) \lor \big(\neg P \land \neg Q\big)
$$

There are many ways to say $P\Leftrightarrow Q$ in words. Among the most common are the following:

- *$P$ is equivalent to $Q$*

- *$P$ if and only if $Q$*

- *If $P$ then $Q,$ and if $Q$ then $P$*

- *$P$ implies $Q$, and $Q$ implies $P$*
